work.title: Vita S. Lucae junioris (Steiriotae)

paragraphs.text: Luke, good in all things and great, was himself a shoot of Hellas, or rather, I should say, her ornament and her truly beloved delight; and I will add that he was also her crown of glory. For he did not show himself ungrateful to the land that bore him, but repaid her richly with splendid and conspicuous honors. His forebears came originally from the island of Aegina, the Aegina that lies in the Aegean gulf. Judging the constant raids of the sons of Hagar to be unbearable, they themselves and

all the inhabitants were forced to abandon the dear soil of their homeland. They became emigrants and were scattered, each to a different city, as if they had taken stepmothers in place of a mother. Some went to the city of Cecrops, others to that of Pelops, others to that of Cadmus, and others elsewhere, and there they were compelled to make their homes.

The forebears of the divine Luke moved into the province of Phocis, that is, of Chrysos, and pitched the tents of their sojourn by a certain coastal mountain called Ioannou. But at that time, by judgments known to Him "whose judgments are a great deep," the sons of Ishmael ruled the sea and raided every gulf, beach and shore, and they had already begun to attack this region too, so the family was compelled to withdraw once more. They came to a certain harbor called Bathys, a well-suited and calm place, and settled there. They spent no short time there, and were granted the birth of the divine Luke's father. They honored him with the name of the first of the martyrs, and naturally gave the child an upbringing worthy of that name. But they moved on again from there and settled in a certain village called Kastorion. There they rested a little from their wandering, hoping to find some consolation for their exile. This did not come at once, but it came not long afterward. For God, who shared Jacob's exile and made him rich instead of poor, and who caused the man who had once crossed the stream of the Jordan with only a staff to return with a multitude of cattle and flocks, also plainly blessed their livestock and the rest of their property and made it grow, so that not only were they seen to be inferior to no one in wealth, but they far surpassed the natives. The boy Stephen passed beyond childhood and reached his prime, and when he came of age to marry, they joined him to a wife named Euphrosyne, who came from the same homeland and was likewise of good family. By her Stephen had seven children. The first was Theodore, and after him came Maria. The fourth is named Kale, who has also told us these things and still pursues the contests of monastic life. Epiphanius was the fifth; he too took up the solitary life, followed a way of life in harmony with his profession, and passed over to Him whom he loved. The
other two children departed this life before they had passed beyond their tender years. But the third was the one who was most divine in all things

Thereafter love of God and of stillness took hold of him again and made him forget everything else and belong to himself alone. Since his mother no longer opposed this, he made his way to the mountain mentioned before, the one the locals rustically call Ioannitza. He went around to the side facing the sea, where there is a shrine of the wonderful brothers Cosmas and Damian, and there he pitched his ascetic tent. What contests and labors he showed there, what a battle against the belly and sleep, or rather against the [?], cannot be told accurately, nor would those who told it be believed without doubt, so far does the matter exceed belief. He had never yet received the perfecting grace of the divine and great habit, and he longed for it greatly; by the providence of the Good One he was found worthy of this too, and in this way. Two monks, adorned with the grey hair of old age, or rather adorning their grey hair with virtue, were making the journey to elder Rome, as if sent on some mission. He received them hospitably and kindly, then shared his intention with them and begged them very earnestly about the matter. They saw that the vessel was worthy to receive it and did not delay. They hastily performed the customary rites over him, clothed him in the apostolic and blessed habit, and invested him with the emblems of the narrow and hard way, the way that leads to life. Or rather, what he already was in his deeds, they now showed through the habit as well. But I will also tell the wonder worked for those who performed this holy rite, the monks I mean. For they were [?] … but [?] meanwhile the [?] of the provisions, which knows a little

… of necessities at the great Luke's place. There was nothing worthy of his generous mind and intention, especially for such guests, who had brought him so great a good. What then did He do who opens His rich right hand and fills every living thing with His good pleasure? They were sitting on the shore, as the sun was already spreading its clear rays, gazing out at the gentle breezes over the waves. Then a large fish leapt high into the air and landed at their feet, flopping and jumping most delightfully, as if inviting those present to prepare it. They gave thanks to their Guardian and Provider of food, and marveled at His providence. Then, in the hearing of all, the great one said: "A man is coming to us carrying a great and heavy load and enduring much toil." So he spoke, and soon after he rose from among them, went off into the mountain, and made darkness his hiding place. They marveled and wondered what the saying meant, who this load-bearing man was, and what his load might be, for they thought he was speaking of a bodily weight. And behold, the man himself came into view of them all, alone, plainly dressed, lightly girded, carrying no load at all. He called for the saint by name, saying that he urgently needed his help. Those with the saint's sister told him to wait: "He has gone away, as you see, and is not with us now. If you want to see him, you must wait." He insisted that he would not leave before meeting him, and the seventh day passed. At last the saint came out, like another Moses, as from a thick darkness, from the inner sanctuary of his stillness. As soon as he saw the man, he made his look stern and his voice harsh and unlike his usual one, and said, "What have you to do with this untrodden desert? Why have you left the cities and come to the mountains? Why have you left the shepherds and chief shepherds in the churches and come seeking rustic and unlearned men? How did you dare to come into my sight, and why did you not shudder at divine justice, guilty as you are of such outrages?" At this the man was seized with trembling, tears streamed down his cheeks, and his tongue was bound with fetters of fear. The saint went on: "How long will you keep silent," he said, "and not publish your sin before all, before shepherds and chief shepherds [?]

and uncover the unjust murder, so that by becoming your own accuser you may in this way appease a little the Divine, which by nature hates evil?" With difficulty the man forced himself to speak, his breath coming in gasps and broken: "Why, man of God," he said, "do you demand to learn from me what you yourself were taught before I spoke, by the grace that dwells in you? For what I did in secret was not hidden from you. Nonetheless I yield to your command: I speak, and I publish the evil that was done." With these words he openly confessed his sin, going through every detail: how and where and for what reason he had killed his traveling companion. Then he fell at the saint's feet, begging not to be cast aside. The saint took pity on him and quickly raised him up. He admonished and encouraged him and secured him with penances he could bear, enjoining this above all: that he go to the tomb of the murdered man, pour out many tears there, and lavishly perform the memorials of the third, ninth and fortieth days for him, making prostrations there, no fewer than three thousand if possible. Or rather, he was to lament the sin all his life and keep it before him, writing it on the tablets of his soul. With this charge he sent him home, having instilled in him a pure knowledge of the good and condemnation of his sin, and the man promised to show great repentance. When the saint had completed his seventh year in the desert at Ioannitza, he too, against his will, became an exile along with everyone else. For Symeon, ruler of the Scythian nation (we usually call them Bulgarians), broke his treaties with the Romans and advanced against the whole mainland, girded with our sins as with an arm strong for battle. He enslaved and plundered, robbing some of life and others of freedom, and making them pay tribute. So some were shut up in the cities as in prisons or garrisons, while others escaped to Euboea and the Peloponnese. At that time the villagers around the man of God also crossed over to the neighboring islands. But envy got there first and brought an unexpected danger upon them. For while they thought they were living safely with the righteous man, the Bulgarians stole a boat they happened upon, fell on them suddenly and almost destroyed them all. Only a few swam away, and the great one was among them; so they managed to escape their hands. When they returned, he found a boat and crossed over with his whole family and his acquaintances to

Corinth. He was just then growing a beard on his cheeks, and had the bloom of youth, the season that is fitted for virtue [?]. Even at that age, love of learning drew him, for the sake of reading the sacred scriptures. So he went and gave himself to a school, but he was to share little of the benefit there. For he saw that the boys were unruly, receiving the finest lessons but not preparing fine souls to receive them. He could not bear this, and withdrew at once. So he went out into the country towns. And since he heard that at Patras in Achaea there was a Stylite practicing a loftier way of life, he had the thought of going there to serve him. While he was turning this over, an embassy was sent to him from the stylite at Zemena, asking him to come and live with him, and if not as an equal [?], then to be placed under him and accept the work of serving him. He gladly received the embassy, since he loved to be ruled rather than to rule, knowing that this is more profitable for a young man, and knowing well, besides, what exaltation comes from humility. So he gladly went to him and very eagerly undertook the service. From then on there was no kind of service that he did not hasten to do himself, for he considered it the greatest loss and dishonor to leave any task of service to someone else. Once, when someone was reviling the stylite with an unbridled tongue and mocking him, Luke happened to be present. He took it so hard, and his soul burned with such zeal, that he forgot his silence and decorum and his great modesty and calm, and was compelled to use harsher words against that shameless reviler, correcting the rash slanderer with a well-trained tongue that moved at the right moment. But the man was very insolent, and suffering from no small or curable ailment, he showed at once that he needed stronger discipline. Unable to bear the rebuke, he struck the sanctified man on the jaw with his foul hand. But vengeance followed close on his heels: "from heaven judgment was made heard," the hidden virtue was brought to light, and the wickedness was rightly punished. For as soon as the insulter struck, he himself was struck far more heavily with a demonic blow. He lay on the ground shaking and convulsing, wretchedly suffering what the possessed suffer. And why should I not tell the more fearful part, which is worthy of many tears and can frighten those who do not spare their tongues? He remained so to the end, "delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh," as Paul says, "so that the spirit may be saved." The reason was this: he ought rather to have been a corrector of others when they behaved foolishly, for he was a priest, giving exhortation by word and by life; but he was foolish himself, so that

he became a stumbling block to others and an open disgrace to his rank. It was wholly alien and utterly contrary to the enemy's envy to let the divine Luke serve under the Stylite to the end, rather than move every stone to bar him from this good work. So the adversary of the good did not stop doing everything he could until he succeeded and separated them from each other. What was the pretext for the separation and the parting? The official entrusted with the care of the harbors, who did not allow ships to cross to the borders of Hellas because of enemy attacks, caught him trying to cross in a boat and beat him with unbearable blows. After this he decided to live on his own, and from then on the chapel of the divine martyr Prokopios held him, living under God and clinging to his ever-beloved stillness. But there too a violent rainstorm broke and overturned the little hut he lived in, and made him leave again, though he did not want to. Perhaps God arranged this for good, so that by lingering too long in the Peloponnese he would not wrong his homeland by depriving her of such a plant and [?]. For not much time passed before the wicked Symeon, the cause of the shedding of much Christian blood, departed from among men. His rule passed to Peter, his son, who proved to be heir to his glory and his wealth but not likewise to his cruelty and hatred of mankind; he was far removed from it, and in that respect had nothing of that blood and kinship. He at once said farewell to blood and wars and embraced peace with us. Then sword and spear and every weapon made of iron were, to speak with the prophet, beaten into sickles and adzes. And when everyone was returning safely to their own cities and villages and to their very hearths, the divine Luke too returned longingly to his beloved stillness at Ioannitza. He held to the same labors of virtue, or even greater ones, while taking care to relieve the labors of others, especially those of travelers, through his kindly hospitality. So, hearing that the bishop of Corinth was going up to the queen of cities and was to stop somewhere nearby to rest a little from his toil, he went out to meet him, not with empty hands but bringing gifts. They were small, but given with a great and generous intent, for he brought the best of what he had and kept nothing better for himself: vegetables of many kinds from the garden he had labored over, for the bishop himself and for the clergy and officials with him. When the bishop learned from them who he was, where he lived, and what kind of life he led, he did what a man who loves virtue

and is passionately devoted to divine things would do. Thinking pomp and the measure of rank a paltry thing, he considered it a great matter to see the hut of a poor man, though one who was not poor in spiritual things. So he came, and taking in the loftiness of his life [?], he marveled at what is truly worth marveling at: not wealth and splendor, but voluntary and self-chosen poverty. For this reason he was eager to present the man with gold. For we are accustomed to give more eagerly, not to those who are in need, but to those who are above needing. So he told the closest of his attendants to give it to him. But Luke refused to take it, saying, "I did not come to you, master, in need of gold, but of prayers and teaching. For what is gold to us, who have chosen to live like this? Give me, then, what I need and greatly thirst for: teach me, ignorant and rustic as I am, how I ought

The archbishop was deeply grieved that his gift was refused. He thought that what had happened showed contempt not for the gift but rather for himself, and that Luke had refused it not because he had no need of it, but because he did not approve of the giver. So, sorely pained at heart, he said, "Why do you thrust us away like this along with the gift? I too am a believer, even if a sinner, and a bishop, even if unworthy. Since you wish to imitate Christ in all things, why do you not imitate Him in this? He too accepted the offerings of the pious who wished to give, and the money box is an unfailing witness to this. Surely, even if you need nothing of what is given, you will hand it on to others who do need it. But as it is, so far as you are concerned, the commandment to do good is something vain and senseless; and in this way you maim a noble disposition, which joins love of mankind to love of God. In short, you take away an opportunity that can both relieve the heaviness of poverty and become a way of salvation for many." When the man of God heard this, he saw that he must not refuse to accept any longer, lest he gain a reputation for conceit and cause the bishop excessive grief. So he took no more than a single coin, and gave in return a wealth of prayers. Then, with what contrition of mind you can imagine, he asked the archbishop: "Tell me, master, how can we, who for the multitude of our sins live in the mountains and deserts, partake of the divine and awesome mysteries? For you see that we lack not only a congregation but also a priest." The archbishop warmly approved the question. "You do well, Father," he said, "to inquire about a good and very great matter. For the good, as they say, is not good when it is not done well. A priest should, if possible, be present. But when he must of necessity be absent, place the vessel of the presanctified gifts on the holy table

if it is a chapel; if it is a cell, on a perfectly clean stool. Then spread out the cloths and set the holy portions on it. Burn incense and sing the psalms of the Typika, or the Trisagion, together with the Creed. Then kneel three times, and with your hands held back, partake with your mouth of the precious body of Christ our God, saying the Amen. Instead of the consecrated wine, drink a cup of wine. That cup, however, must not afterward be shared for anyone else's use. Then wrap the remaining portions again in the little veil inside the vessel, taking every precaution that no pearl falls and is trodden underfoot." The great one listened and gave thanks for these instructions. Then the archbishop went on with his journey, and Luke held to his prayers and his stillness. It was the great one's custom, on the feast of Palms, to climb to the ridge of the mountain at daybreak, holding the divine weapon of the cross in his hands and crying aloud, "Lord, have mercy." Once, as he was going up, the enemy who always envies the good wanted somehow to hinder this God-loving purpose. He made a viper come out of its hole and fasten on the toe of the saint's foot. That is what the wicked one did, using the reptile as his instrument. But what did the good man do? He acted as his good soul moved him, as befits a good and God-loving man. The great one at once bent down, took hold of his foot [?] and of the beast, and said, "Neither will you harm me, nor I you. Let us each go our own way, since we are both works of one Creator, without whose consent and will we can do nothing at all." So

…when he had said this, the viper at once let go of his foot and took the path leading to its hole. The divine man remained unharmed, and suffered no harm at all from the bite. An imperial official was sent to the regions of Africa by the one who then held the imperial sceptre. When he had reached Corinth, the gold he was carrying for imperial services was stolen. Since the crime had been committed by someone in the dead of night and was hidden, the streets were searched, as usually happens in such cases. The squares were searched too, and everyone under suspicion was put to interrogation. But when every effort proved fruitless and there was no hope of finding the gold, a heavy despondency took hold of the man. After a good deal more: when they had eaten enough and were eager to take their delight in the remembrance of God rather than in the food, the great man suddenly raised his eyes. Fixing them on one of those standing by, he called him by name and summoned him. When the man stood near him, the seer said to him: "Why were you about to bring death on yourself and danger on your master by daring to lay hands on imperial money? Go quickly and bring us the gold you buried, if you care at all to obtain pity and pardon." The man heard, and his tongue was as if bound with a fetter, and he could say nothing at all in reply, since his conscience bore witness against him and spoke with the saint. So he hastened to set right the work of darkness by the light of repentance. He fell down at once and clasped the saint's feet, as though cleansing hands defiled by theft. He confessed the wrong he had done and fervently begged for pardon. He obtained it, for this was the way of that soul: not only to reveal the wound but also to offer the cure as quickly as possible. He went off at once and brought back the gold intact, before the eyes of all who were watching. In that place, however, the saint had to bear many disturbances, because many people came every day and were eroding his love of stillness and calm. He wished to withdraw from there and move to more deserted places. Yet he would not let himself follow [?], since he knew how to resist his own will and never simply to give in to it. For this reason he decided to send the monk who served him, Germanus by name, to Corinth, to a man then renowned for his virtue. This was Theophylact the Wise, who was a teacher of secular learning, but no less taught virtue by his deeds to those who loved what is good. So he sent to him, seeking to learn what he ought to do: whether to stay where he was and put up with being troubled by many, or rather to choose places inaccessible to the crowd and scarce in people. Theophylact said: "The saying of the divine Arsenius is excellent and
must prevail. For he said, 'Flee from men and be saved,' and again, 'Flee, be silent,'

When the wondrous Luke heard this, he left the region of Ioannitzes [?] and moved to a place called Kalabion in the local tongue. It was not only well suited to stillness but also situated in good air, so he welcomed it gladly, and while he lived there his soul rejoiced. They say the blessed man spent three years there. Then, when the nation of the Turks was overrunning Hellas, he too went over, together with the surrounding villages, to the nearby islet called Ampelon, which is extremely parched and waterless. For the noble man it became a training ground of virtue and a source of good fruits. Every day he went and fetched water and gave it to the crowds. Nor was it only water: when he had wine and grain he shared them too, and sometimes he went fishing and gave the fish away freely. When the people wanted to cross over to the Peloponnese, no longer expecting to see Hellas freed from the nations, he held them back, saying: "This is a spring cloud, brothers, and any moment now it will be scattered, and clear skies will shine on us more brightly than before. Even if the West is not wholly allowed to enjoy a deep calm, you will suffer the same as the Israelites. Their readiness for wickedness was hard to heal, not to say entirely incurable, and the One who knows all things, knowing this, did not let the son of Nun wholly destroy the nations bordering on Zion. He did this so that when they sinned they would have their correctors at their doors. It was not that God lacked some other way to discipline them, but that by always seeing the whip hanging over them they might live more securely." The man of God lived on this islet for three more years. He often went without not only comforts but even water itself. Whenever fierce winds blew and the sea could not be sailed, so that he could not cross over to draw water, he stayed like that for a long time, wasting away with thirst. What is more, the enemy devised yet another blow against him. He brought upon his genital parts an itching so severe and savage that it nearly drove him to cut them off. What treatment, then, did he use for

such an evil? Continual prayer to God and to the saint who lies there in the body. This saint appeared to him in a dream and showed him a herb, saying: "By this you will find healing for what pains you. But know clearly that by doing so you will lose the reward owed for your endurance." When he woke, he did not prove a poor judge in choosing what was profitable. He did not prefer relief from something that would trouble him for a little while to an eternal recompense, but chose to go on suffering. So it remained until the Lord of knowledge, who credits the intention alone with the completion of the deed, healed the affliction in the way he knows, and stored up perfect rewards for his athlete in the age to come. Now it is time to speak [?] of his move as well, and how he left this islet and moved to the place that also saw him die and is now enriched with his sacred relics. Those who had shared the saint's flight and had received much care from him on this island learned what kind of man he was in virtue, and wanted to have him near them. So they came to him. What did they not say, what did they not do of all that could persuade a soul attached to its habits and quite reasonably averse to moving! They led him off to the place, for the present only to look at it, on the understanding that if it did not suit him he would return to his former dwelling. Then they stood around him and said: "How long will you linger on the coasts, troubled by all the noise from the ships and all the noise from passers-by? Do you see what sort of place this is where you are standing? How mild, how delightful, free of all noise, and almost inaccessible to men! Besides, it has plenty of the purest water, enough both to quench thirst and to irrigate vegetables and plants. You will find nothing lacking or unworthy of what you desire, and you will have us too, ready to serve you in every way." So Luke accepted them and their proposal, and he loved the place as one shown him by God and chose to live there for the rest of his life. Then he cleared the spring of the surrounding undergrowth and made its water flow clearer and more abundantly. Constantly tending and clearing the ground and planting all kinds of plants, he made it like a most beautiful paradise, pleasing not only to the taste but also to the eyes. His cell, however, he did not set near the garden and the spring, but as far away as possible, among the thick shrubs, so that it would not be easily visible to many. For his aim was always to cut off every occasion for vainglory, and to be, and be thought, dead to the present world rather than alive. Pothos, whom everyone knows, happened to be entrusted with the government of Hellas as its strategos. While living at Thebes, he too experienced in fact the grace

that dwelt with the great man. Byzantium was then in no small turmoil, because a plot to usurp the throne had been hatched against the emperor of the time, Constantine the Good. Everyone who had given even slight grounds for suspicion was being rounded up there. So Pothos, whom I have mentioned, was summoned by letters from his wife: "Count everything you have in hand as nothing and come to the Queen City as quickly as you can. For the emperor is eager for your presence, and there is also the death of your dearest child." [?] These things made him deeply gloomy and threw his thoughts into great conflict. His child's death gripped him and urged him to go up; but he feared the times and suspected that if he went up he might fall into danger, especially since he had been told to come not by the emperor at all, but only by his wife. As he wavered like this, torn between two passions, longing and fear, one of the officials came to him and mentioned the divine Luke. "If you go and talk with this man," he said, "and consult him about the matter, nothing will be left in doubt for you about what you should do, and you will know clearly what is to your advantage." When the strategos heard this, he did not leave the matter to time and delay, but made it his first concern to come before the saint. When he met him, he heard nothing ambiguous like the Pythian oracles, but what would benefit him, plainly and clearly. For the saint spoke with fitting bearing and composure, neither seeking to make a display nor overawed by the man's office as something great and marvellous: "Go up to Constantinople, lord strategos, without grief or fear, and the Lord will make all your crooked paths straight. The emperor will look on you with favourable eyes and will even honour you, and you yourself will see the child well and free of every ailment." The strategos heard these words as from a prophetic, God-inspired tongue. He did not doubt at all what he had heard, and set out on his way. When he arrived and saw that everything had come to pass, he did not hide the wonder in silence, but passed it on as a fine story to the ears of many. And the case of the illustrious and admired Krinites: how could one fail to commit it to writing and memory, without incurring the charge of envy and malice, or of negligence? He too had likewise been entrusted with the government of Hellas, and as he travelled there and drew near Larissa, his ears were filled with stories about the saint,

or rather about his wonders, and he conceived a longing to see him and talk with him. So when he had reached the region of Thebes, he at once sent for him and summoned him, and the saint followed the messenger without delay. He found Krinites reclining at table, since it was the time of the midday meal. When Krinites learned of his arrival and gave permission, the saint too came in and became one of the diners. He rose with the others when they rose and set off to return, without, as it happened, being granted even a brief word by the man who had so warmly summoned him. At this grief took hold of the saint, not for himself, for who loved obscurity more than he? It was for Krinites, and for the venerable habit and name of monks, which had been treated with such contempt in his person. So he went out to one of the strategos's servants and said: "As you hope to enjoy life and salvation, hold nothing back but report this to the strategos: Why did you make me leave my cell and come here? Why did you put me to so much labour for nothing? Why did you force a lover of the desert to come to the city? You did not think me worth a word, you gave me no greeting, you did nothing else that a man who loves virtue and lays claim to even a little piety ought to do." When the great man had said this and charged him again to explain everything to the strategos, he went out to the monastery in the suburb, to the monk Antony. When all this had been reported, the strategos, being in truth a reasonable and moderate man, understood that he had not done what was right and blamed himself severely for his negligence in a matter that deserved care. So he hastened, by the swiftness of his repentance, to heal the fault he had committed through inattention. He mounted a horse at once and came to the saint. First he offered a warm and heartfelt apology for his error and was quickly granted pardon. Then he told those present to withdraw and talked with him alone, prolonging the conversation until evening. And what came of it? He was bound to the saint in a love so warm that his soul clung to him, to use David's words, and he did not want to be without him for even the briefest time. Indeed he most eagerly served and spent for his every need and service. In the building of the church of the gloriously victorious martyr Barbara, too, he contributed what was most essential. When he had to return to Byzantium, since his term of office was already coming to an end, he came to the saint and asked to receive his prayers as companions for the road, and begged not to be forgotten after his departure. The saint said: "But you will not see the Queen City now, for God still wants you in the West." So he spoke. The other set out on his journey, and when he was already near Larissa, he was turned back again and found what had been said confirmed. For an imperial letter at once

[?] appointed him strategos and governor of the Peloponnese. This too is worthy of wonder. But his prediction about Crete comes close to being beyond belief, even though it has abundant truth to witness to it. Almost twenty years beforehand he foretold both that the island would be taken and under whom the capture would happen, saying plainly: "Romanos subdues Crete." Since the elder Romanos was then ruling the empire when he made this prediction, one of those present asked: "Is it the one who reigns now?" "Not this one," he said, "but another." The monk Pankratios told me that a voice from above would regularly come to the saint [?] about attacks of the nations, so that he would be the first of all to withdraw and hide, in order to spare his neighbours from capture, as he himself said when asked. For everyone heeded him as a prophet. Unless they first saw him turn to flight, no one at all would leave their work or their house; they disregarded the report as false and nothing sound

Once, when the voice had come in this way and we had fled, I was with the Father and the two of us had gone into a cave together. Two wandering women came to us when the sun was already sinking to the west. The Father took pity on them, since besides the flight it was also winter, and did not think it right to drive them away. They were taken in with us and given what care was possible. When it was time to sleep, he gave us one side, lay down himself on the other, and let the women stay in the middle because of the cold. He passed the night like a child beside its mother, or as though stones or logs were lying beside him, without a single thought [?] stealing into his mind at all. So completely did simplicity and dispassion hold that angel on earth in their bosom, like a mother. Philip was the brother of the monk Theodosius, who was one of the monks living with the saint. This Philip was a layman, honoured with a worldly dignity (we usually call such men spatharioi), and he used to visit the great man rather often because of his close bond with his brother. Once, when he was coming as usual, the great man saw him with those eyes with which he had seen him, and said graciously to Theodosius: "Prepare whatever is needed to receive a guest, for your brother is coming to dine with us." At the Father's words joy and amazement together took hold of Theodosius, and at once he kept watching the highways, streets and lanes, expecting his brother. When it was already evening, he arrived,

bringing with him whatever provisions were needed. A table was prepared, and all reclined together with the great man. There was nothing set out there that was not eaten by all alike, because of the surpassing beauty of love. When they had eaten in this way and encouraged one another, and had also completed the customary rule after supper, they went to sleep. When they had had only a little of it, the Father at once got them up, and the others were occupied with the synaxis. But Philip's brother, knowing that he was unused to such standing, labour and vigil, let him lie down again, at least until the end of the opening hymns and the so-called stichology. But when the bed received him again, it made him wrestle with many thoughts, "to be in labour with toil and give birth," in David's words, "to iniquity." He supposed the divine man to be a glutton and a drunkard and a hypocrite feigning piety. This came first of all from the one who secretly sows evil seeds in our souls. But it also came from Philip's own small and ignoble mind, which simply judged everything by appearances and could not conceive of anything great or lofty. He did not see that the saint's partaking of what was set before him was not gluttony or love of fine food, but a higher purpose. On the one hand it came from an abundance of love, as we have already shown, the lesser being disregarded for the sake of gaining the greater; for what is abstinence from food compared with such preeminence of love? On the other hand it was so that, through an excess of humility, he might rather seem to be just what Philip, from great dullness and confusion of mind, took him to be. That this was so, and that Philip was dreaming wrongly and had wandered far from the truth, the faithful witness in heaven showed plainly. As Philip was turning these things over and chattering away in his thoughts, sleep took hold of him, and in a dream he saw two young men. Their beauty and the radiance streaming from their faces could neither be described in words nor endured by the eyes. They stood by him with a hostile look that declared bitterness of soul, and said: "Why do you trouble yourself with these thoughts? Why do you lay charges against the blameless? Lift up your eyes, you who look downward, and see what honour has been granted to this man, whom you judge a deceiver and a hypocrite who brings shame on the holy habit of monks." Then he raised his eyes toward the one they were pointing to, and saw something great and wonderful. A precious purple cloth was spread on the ground, and above it stood the great man, shining wonderfully and ineffably in his form and his garments alike, and appearing wholly as light itself. When sleep released Philip, he went, trembling and changed, to where the Fathers were holding the synaxis. He explained everything, both what he himself had turned over while awake on his bed and what he had seen in a dream, supernaturally

…saw it. He was pardoned, and he still goes on proclaiming the miracle and rightly condemning himself for having so wrongly condemned the righteous man. The godly man had said farewell to the coastal regions, come down to the place called Soterion and built his ascetic hut there. When he was finishing his seventh year in it, he knew in advance that his blessed end was at the door. He told no one about it. Instead he left his cell as if on some necessary errand and went round to all his friends, neighbours and acquaintances. He took leave of each of them, kissed their lips, eyes and face, and said, "Pray for me, brothers, pray; for it is uncertain whether we shall see one another again." After the saint had gone round to everyone in this way, he returned to his own cell and lived for three more months. First a mild illness crept up on him. Then the fever attacked him more violently, and when the eighth day had passed it became clear to all that he was leaving the body and going to God, whom he had loved. The people living in the villages round about learned of this. The winter was severe, and so much snow had fallen that the roads were almost impassable and the houses could hardly be reached. Even so, nothing kept them from going to him. They streamed in all together and stayed with him until the ninth hour, with no thought at all of food or of going back. They all stood intent on him, looking at his cheerful face, longing to hear his dearest voice and his last words and to share in his prayer, and unable to bear the parting. I mean, for now, the parting from his bedside, when they had to stop seeing him and go home. As for the final parting after death, what a blow they took from it and how they suffered in their souls for his sake, they showed by the tears that ran down without ceasing. At last he embraced them all, prayed that good things might be theirs, and sent them away against their will, groaning mournfully and deeply grieved. [?] The priest Gregory, however, stayed behind, and the great man asked him the time. Gregory told him that the sun was setting, and Luke understood that he too, that fair star, was now setting. "[?]," he said, "say the evening prayers quickly." Gregory did as he was told. Then, thinking he should ask about the necessary arrangements, he asked where Luke would like to be laid after his death. Luke took this badly. "Is it not a plain disgrace," he said, "for you to seem not to know about this? You must tie my feet with ropes and throw me into one of the ravines. If I am good for nothing else, at least I shall be food for the wild beasts." The priest was not put off by this at all. He asked again, very earnestly, to learn about the burial, and tears came along with his words, for he did not want to act against Luke's wishes even after his death. "The place where I am lying,"

he said, "dig it up, and you will find baked bricks. Lift them out, tidy the place a little, and see that dust is returned to dust. Then lay the bricks on the surface of the ground. For God intends," he said, "for reasons that are hidden and known to him alone, to glorify this place until the end of the age, as crowds of the faithful gather here and glorify his divine name." When he had said this, he embraced Gregory and those with him. Finally he raised his eyes on high, said, "Into your hands, Lord, I commit my spirit," and gave up his blessed [?]

At dawn the priest called together the villagers from the neighbourhood. He dug up the place and adorned it as well as he could. When he had performed the customary rite, he laid the holy body in it like a kind of wealth. He did not do this sparingly or meanly, as if the treasure were to lie there for himself alone, but so that it might be a blessing shared by all who love Christ. Then he covered the ground above with the bricks, as he had been told, and left. Six months after the Father had fallen asleep, a eunuch monk named Cosmas, who came from the land of the Paphlagonians, was travelling to Italy. When he had reached the region of Chrysos, he decided to rest his body there for a while. As he slept, a divine dream came to him. He told the local people about it and heard from them: "You must end your journey here. It is God's will that you serve the divine and new Luke; that is why he arranged for you to set out on this road." Without hesitating at all, as though drawn by a divine hand, Cosmas was led to the saint's cell. Standing there, he saw how delightful the place was and how well suited to stillness. He was very pleased, and he promised God to live there from then on. At once he saw that the area around the holy tomb was bare and neglected, and he gave it some modest care for the time being. He raised the tomb so that it stood above the ground and adorned it with local stone slabs. He set railings around it to enclose it, and so made it impossible to walk on or touch, except for those who wished to approach it faithfully and with great reverence. Two years later some of Luke's disciples saw the healings gushing forth there like spring waters. They judged that they would not be good children of a good Father unless they were seen to repay him for their upbringing, as it were, by giving him even after his end what was due to him after his end.

So they immediately set about building cells and a church. First they eagerly completed the church of the divine martyr Barbara, which had been roughly built, and adorned it as well as they could. Then they built small dwellings, enough of them and of different shapes, for common use and for receiving guests. After that they changed the very cell that held the great man's tomb from its former appearance and beautifully transformed it into a holy oratory in the shape of a cross. In this way the blessed man's words were fulfilled, both about this place and about the crowds who would come together to it. There was a woman whose hands and feet could not move. They could be seen attached to the rest of her body and keeping their proper shape, but they would not work for her; each one refused its proper service. As far as they were concerned, she might have been thought dead rather than alive. On top of so great an evil, and even heavier than what has been described, her son, whom she had hoped to have as her comfort and as a help in what she lacked, was himself possessed by a demon. He was constantly lying on the ground in convulsions. Her relatives pitied her misfortune. They put her on a donkey like a lifeless load and held her on, and they brought her to the new Siloam, the tomb of blessed Luke, with her son following her. They left the two of them there and went back. But how inscrutable are God's judgments! The saint passed her over and kept putting off her healing for a long time. In the end the woman grew weary with the waiting, gave up hope of a cure, and was thinking of going home. But O your ineffable goodness, Christ, and the wonder beyond words that you worked for her! A little earlier the saint's tomb had poured out fragrant myrrh like a spring. The sacristan had carefully collected it, put it into one of the lamps and hung that lamp by the holy tomb. Now, at midday [?], the woman was sitting near the tomb, and no one else was there except her son. He said quietly to her, "Look, I am going to get up and drink what is in this lamp." His mother tried to stop him. "No, child," she said, "the sacristan is short-tempered. He might even whip us and drive us out." "No," he said, "I will do what I have in mind." At once he got up, grabbed the lamp and poured its contents into his mouth. What happened next was simply this: the boy immediately began rolling on the ground in convulsions.

And the mother… but do not let the miracle slip past your ears. Pay attention, for the most delightful part is about to be told. The mother was in great distress and longed to help her dearest child, and then, O strange event, O wonder beyond words! She was no longer without hands or feet as before, but proved fully able to use both. She leapt up on her feet, and with her hands she held up her son and raised him. He too was now in his right mind and free of the demon that had afflicted him so terribly. So the woman unexpectedly received a double grace, and so great a one, within a single hour. Overcome by joy and wonder, she did not know what to make of what had happened to her, and she had nothing to offer in return for such a grace. So, having given up on any other way, she repaid it from her own household and with her own self.
